 First Rain
 Trudy Wischemann 
 Published October 28, 2026  •  
 4:02 pm 
 On Oct. 21, three weeks into the new water year, we got our first rain. Amid flash flood warnings, people held their breaths as it turned into just the rain we needed.
 I’m writing it down so that I can remember the blessing of it: the first drops on the windshield; the instant change in the smell of the air, going from dust to damp; the sudden need for a sweatshirt and socks. The peace of it, feeling that all is right with the world, at least meteorologically. We begin again with the arrival of the first rain.
 The timing couldn’t have been better. I was in Visalia for the fourth quarterly meeting of the Tulare County Flood Control Commission to ask for immediate help preparing for flooding in Alpaugh and Allensworth. With clouds in the sky, it was much easier to think about the possibility of floods than it would have been the day before.   
 Afterward, outside the board chambers, I was talking with a couple of the commissioners when the conversation turned to the floods of February 1986.
 I have been reading an amazing book about the evolution of flood control in the Sacramento Valley, historian Robert Kelly’s “Battling the Inland Sea” (1989). The first special districts created in California were reclamation districts, which allowed landowners to create farmland “reclaimed” from of marshy wetlands by walling off annual floodwaters with levees. These districts grew quickly in the Sacramento Valley, the Delta and the Tulare Lake Basin. After a decade of private levee building, however, one problem discovered in the Sacramento was that these levees increased flooding outside the reclamation districts. After many decades of trial and error, a valley-wide system had to be devised, dedicating certain lands to floodways, leaving farms and cities relatively dry.
 Yet sometimes things still go wrong. The flood of 1986 clearly is what caused Robert Kelly to write the book. The photo fronting the title page is of a 16-year-old boy in the bow of an aluminum rowboat, one hand clinging to the top branches of a drowned leafless tree, the other holding onto the boat’s edge, his golden retriever nuzzling the back of his neck. The Feather River’s surging flows had caught him, and he clung there for hours before they could be rescued.   
 He and his dog were some of the lucky ones. On another page is quoted a Sacramento computer technician, who said the worst part of that flood “was the sound of dogs and cats who howled and screamed as they drowned.” As a levee breached on the Yuba River, a 12-foot wall of water burst through, sucking a half-acre peach grove with it. Hundreds of homes ended up 10-15 feet underwater. Among those who survive such floods, many people never recover emotionally.   
 I was living 10 miles west of Davis then, in a one-room shack on the plain south of Putah Creek. The water came up around my front door, but not inside, so I lost nothing, was merely inconvenienced. I remember driving across the Yolo Bypass with water lapping the bottom of the causeway. For a few days it seemed like the rain would never stop. But because the Sacramento River eventually flows through the Delta into San Francisco Bay and out the Golden Gate, everyone knew that this, too, would pass eventually and repairs could begin.   
 To the early settlers of that Valley, when the Sacramento was wall-to-wall, it often seemed like an inland sea. But with huge public effort historically and modern engineering works (plus vigilance maintaining those works, depending on who is in charge), the Sacramento is now a safer valley to inhabit and farm.
 We here, in our essentially closed basin, are still in that more primitive stage of flood control. We have not progressed past our private reclamation district levee system, which walls off flood waters from four major rivers and several minor undammed streams trying to reach the lowest elevations once known as Tulare Lake. Tulare Lake is still needed as the destination of these predictable repeating floods, regardless of where the lowest point shifts in response to overpumping the aquifers.
 It took enormous political will over many decades to transform the flood control system in the Sacramento Valley. As climate change drives our weather into more extreme patterns, we may be forced to work our Basin’s transformation more quickly.
 May the blessing of the first rain make us bolder in wanting to protect and improve our lives here.
 Trudy Wischemann has been a student of floods most of her life. You can send her your dreams of change c/o P.O. Box 1374, Lindsay CA 93247. This column is not a news article but the opinion of the writer and does not reflect the views of the Mid Valley Times newspaper.
